note: The answer declares the standard pH-4.01 buffer 'remains reliable at pH 3.2' which is exactly the prohibited claim that the 4/7/10 buffers are adequate at pH 3 and it makes none of the required points about the 1.68 buffer calibrated range temperature matching or the 0.05 pH-unit check. Unmet: States the usual 4/7/10 buffer set is not sufficient for acidic water and a pH 1.68 (or 2) buffer is needed; States the standard pH procedure is expected to be accurate over roughly pH 1.68 to 10; States the sample pH must fall inside the calibrated range so 4/7/10 does not bracket pH 3.2; States calibration buffers must be within about 10 C of the sample temperature; States a check of the buffer nearest the sample pH should be within about 0.05 pH unit of its value at that temperature or recalibrate

The answer correctly states that below pH 4 standard temperature-compensation factors can be badly wrong and quantifies the error as up to about 50 percent but omits the cause the 'largest source of error' point the 25 °C equilibration check its pass bar and the comment-field recording requirement. Unmet: explains the cause as the hydrogen ion having different transport properties from other ions and contributing a large share of the conductance at low pH; states that at low pH the temperature correction can be the single largest source of error in the measurement; describes the check of comparing the in-situ reading against the same water equilibrated to 25 C; gives the pass bar for that check as within about 5 microsiemens per centimetre at or below 100 or about 3 percent above that; states that if an alternative low-pH compensation method is used the compensation factor has to be recorded in the comment field

The answer correctly attributes the swings to the bailed/decanted method and notes the DO/Eh/temperature restriction but omits the qualified-reporting allowance the in-situ vs recommended parameter split the anoxic/reducing inert-gas restriction and the suction-lift pump warning. Unmet: Explains bailed/decanted samples cannot establish unqualified ambient Eh; acknowledges subsample section permits estimated explicitly qualified reporting; States ORP DO and temperature are required in situ where possible while pH conductivity and turbidity are only recommended; States that in anoxic or reducing groundwater subsample procedures must not be used at all unless handled under inert gas; Warns that a peristaltic or other suction-lift pump also must not be used for ORP or DO because negative pressure volatilises dissolved gases

The answer makes the subsample-qualifier points but effectively permits filling a bottle from the flow-cell outlet violating the must-not item and omits the turbidity storage limits and on-site/time-sensitivity guidance. Unmet: States plainly that a discrete turbidity sample must not be collected from the discharge passing through the flow-through chamber; Gives storage limits: clean amber bottle out of sunlight chilled at or below 4 C held no longer than 24 hours; Notes turbidity is time sensitive and should be measured on site preferably in situ

The answer makes the transport-warming point but omits condensation the other bench biases the requirement to check both methods and the equilibration/particle-association note; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: Identifies condensation on the sample cell as a plausible source of bias when sample water is much colder than air without establishing it as the actual cause; Names the other bench-measurement biases: cell orientation coloured water gas bubbles scratched or dirty sample cells; Explains the preference for in-situ or pumped dynamic measurement while requiring checks of both methods before deciding which reading is reliable; Notes that letting the sample equilibrate to ambient temperature reduces condensation but warming the sample can change particle associations in the water

The answer gives the recording schedule and the items to log (electrode system temperature pH) but omits the in-situ/airtight-flowthrough requirement tubing impermeability and purging thermal-equilibrium drift beyond 30 minutes the slower/asymmetric ORP response and the nearest-10-mV Eh reporting. Unmet: states the measurement must be made in situ with a submersible instrument or through an airtight flowthrough system that eliminates aeration; states the tubing must be relatively impermeable to oxygen the fittings airtight and atmospheric oxygen purged from the tubing and flow channels before measuring; states the reading drifts until thermal equilibrium is reached and that this can take longer than 30 minutes; notes the ORP system responds more slowly than pH and asymmetrically taking longer in one direction than the other; States calculated Eh is reported to the nearest 10 mV.

The answer correctly gives the one-point calibration goal the calibration-checked barometer to 1 mm Hg and the 0.1 C temperature reading but omits the computation from temperature and ionic strength the conductivity-based salinity estimate the timing of manual salinity correction and the recalibration-on-salinity-change point. Unmet: Reported concentration computed from sensor signal with temperature and ionic strength not mg/L directly; Ionic strength for salinity correction estimated from conductivity measurement; Checks droplets on optical module and temperature sensor and recalibrates if present; does not assume unidentified probe is optical; Manual salinity correction applied after calibration and measurement; distinguishes automatic conductivity-based compensation; Manual salinity correction at calibration forces recalibration for each field salinity change

The answer gives the ±0.2 °C accuracy requirement and the comparison against a certified/traceable reference but omits the range-of-use verification vs. adjustment distinction and the faulty-thermistor effect on specific conductance. Unmet: States checking means verifying accuracy across the range of use not adjusting to a standard like pH/conductivity; States a faulty or drifting thermistor in the conductivity cell produces wrong specific conductance values

The answer makes the per-degree range the linear α(t−25) equation the 0.019–0.020 factor and the 25 °C reference point but omits the ±5 percent accuracy statement for 5–35 °C and pH 4–11 and carries no citation to the specific-conductance document. Unmet: States temperature compensation is typically accurate to ±5 percent for 5-35 °C and pH 4-11 without claiming universal invalidity outside that range

The answer invents a discrepancy between the chapters claims the multiparameter chapter is stricter and resolves the imagined conflict by picking a document violating every 'must not' item and making none of the required points. Unmet: States plainly that the two tables give the same stabilisation criteria and do not conflict; States the general field-measurement chapter itself points multiparameter users to the multiparameter chapter for criteria of the same kind; States the criteria are standard sensor stabilisation criteria and that actual sensor accuracy varies by model and manufacturer which is a separate matter; For persistent variability extends equilibration and records additional measurements then reports the median of the final five or more readings or selects a representative final reading using site knowledge and professional judgment documenting the decision

The answer gives no numeric stabilization criteria for any parameter (temperature SC DO pH turbidity) no five-consecutive-readings rule and no 60-second minimum thermal-equilibrium wait so it misses every must-contain point though it avoids the must-not violations. Unmet: temperature criterion about ±0.2 °C; specific conductance criterion ±5 µS/cm at or below 100 ±3% above; dissolved oxygen criterion about ±0.2 mg/L; pH criterion about ±0.1 unit; turbidity stabilization ±0.5 TU or ±5% whichever greater at or below 100 TU; ±10% above 100 TU; criterion judged over five or more consecutive readings; minimum wait in surface water at least 60 seconds for thermal equilibrium; 60 seconds is a minimum and some instruments need longer per manufacturer up to several minutes

The answer correctly gives the EPA daily pre-use calibration and the drift/recalibration-and-qualify rule but omits the sampling-location exemption the sonde deployment/recovery check the DO post-calibration check details and the QA-plan drift-criteria caveat. Unmet: EPA cadence includes end-of-day check except when calibrated at each sampling location under the stated exemption; Continuously deployed sonde calibrated before deployment and checked on recovery; DO post-calibration check done in measurement mode recording DO temperature and barometric pressure against an oxygen-solubility chart; SOP's own drift criteria apply only when the project QA plan does not specify its own

The answer correctly directs a ZoBell's-solution check and notes the expected value is temperature-dependent and looked up from a table but omits the 430 mV value interpolation the 15–30 minute equilibration the 5 mV pass window with reference-electrode correction and the 90-day/4 C stability and no must-not item is violated. Unmet: gives the theoretical ZoBell Eh at 25 C as about 430 mV; states values for temperatures between table rows are interpolated; states the solution and sensors must be left to reach thermal equilibrium on the order of 15 to 30 minutes before the check is read; Gives the check pass window as calculated Eh after adding the appropriate reference-electrode potential to measured potential within 5 mV of the temperature-specific table value; States ZoBell's solution is reported stable for at least 90 days chilled at 4 C; does not invent a 90-day expiry

The answer correctly says the 0.3 mg/L swing exceeds the ±0.2 mg/L tolerance but it mislabels the performance-check value as the stability criterion omits the five-consecutive-reading stabilisation rule the median rules and the ORP note. Unmet: Gives the USGS stabilisation criterion for optical DO as about ±0.2 mg/L across five or more consecutive readings; Allows longer equilibration and additional readings then either the median of the final five or more readings or a representative final reading selected using site knowledge and professional judgment with the decision documented; Gives the median rule as the final three or more readings in surface water or the final five or more in groundwater; Notes that ORP is not covered by that stabilisation table and is instead judged by the potential holding constant over the reading sequence

The answer is a bare refusal that withholds the calibration order and all supporting details the rubric requires making none of the must-contain points. Unmet: states the order does matter and gives temperature first; gives specific conductance next before pH; gives general remaining order pH DO ORP turbidity ion-selective/fluorescence with A6.2 DO-last exception; explains rationale as low to high ionic strength; states conductivity before pH because pH buffers/filling solutions are high ionic strength contamination source; states sensors rinsed three times with deionized water between standards; states sonde calibrated or checked before each field use

The answer correctly covers low ionic strength the incomplete circuit the liquid-junction/ionic-strength mismatch the KCl fix at ~150 µS/cm and a different electrode type but omits the <0.01 pH unit effect the condition that KCl is used only after the normal procedure fails and the warning against stirring the untreated subsample. Unmet: States the KCl addition changes the measured pH by less than about 0.01 unit; States the KCl procedure is used only after the normal procedure has been tried and the reading would not stabilise; Warns against stirring the untreated low-conductance subsample to speed stabilization while permitting gentle swirling to dissolve KCl

The answer gives the pH-downstream-of-conductivity placement but omits the cell-design caveat the keep-close-and-shield-from-sunlight guidance and the design-dependent conductivity probe position; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: States the flow cell should be kept as close to the source water as possible and shielded from direct sunlight; Notes the specific-conductance probe position relative to the pH electrode depends on the flow-cell design

The answer is a bare refusal that withholds the requested explanation making none of the must-contain points though it violates no must-not item. Unmet: Identifies pH dissolved oxygen specific conductance and ORP as potentially affected where their calculations or calibration rely on that temperature sensor; does not assume the pod wiring or compensation configuration; Explains for specific conductance that the reported value is a temperature-corrected number computed from the measured temperature; Explains for dissolved oxygen that the reported concentration is computed from the sensor signal together with temperature; Explains for pH that the buffer values used to calibrate it depend on temperature; Notes that on a multiparameter instrument the temperature sensor typically sits in a different part of the instrument from the pH electrode

The answer refuses the question outright stating it lacks information and makes none of the required table-bound points so it scores 0. Unmet: EPA chart temperature coverage runs to 45 C no value above; USGS table stops at 40.0 C highest tabulated temperature; USGS table extends down to 600 mmHg lower than EPA chart; EPA chart bottoms out around 690 mmHg; Explains different bounds; neither covers temp >40 C and pressure <690 mmHg simultaneously; Only USGS chapter supplies salinity correction factors

The answer gives no solubility figures no 0.03 mg/L difference no Benson and Krause reference and no tolerance comparison so it misses every must-contain point. Unmet: gives the USGS table value at 20.0 C and 760 mmHg as about 9.09 mg/L; gives the EPA chart value at 20 C and 760 mmHg as about 9.06 mg/L; states the difference is 0.03 mg/L and assesses its significance against the applicable procedure; notes the USGS values are generated from the Benson and Krause equations; compares the 0.03 mg/L difference with the USGS saturation-check tolerance of ±0.2 mg/L; advises using the table belonging to whichever protocol the work is being done under consistently rather than mixing them

The answer refuses the A6.8 example-form criteria the rubric asks for so the ±0.1 and ±0.3/75 µS/cm points are missing and no distinction from A6.4's check is drawn though it correctly states A6.4's 0.05 pH-unit final-buffer check. Unmet: Attributes ±0.1 pH unit to the A6.8 example field form's calibration criterion; Attributes ±0.3 pH unit below 75 µS/cm to that example form; Distinguishes the form's conductivity-dependent criteria from A6.4's final-buffer check requiring agreement within 0.05 pH unit of the certified value at calibration temperature

The answer gives the NIST-traceable check and the ±0.2 °C tolerance but omits the contrast with pH calibration the at-least-annual cadence and the probe/temperature-sensor coverage and evaporation point and it declines the interval; no 'must not' item is violated. Unmet: States a temperature sensor is not adjusted to a standard the way a pH/conductivity sensor is; procedure is to verify accuracy across the range of use; Minimum cadence is at least annually; Calibration solution must cover probe and temperature sensor; evaporation of moisture is a DO air-calibration concern

The answer refuses and gives no solubility numbers missing nearly all must-contain points and it violates the must-not item by answering only with the qualitative rule that warm water holds less oxygen and giving no numbers. Unmet: gives freshwater oxygen solubility at ~15 C (~10.0-10.1 mg/L near 760 mmHg); gives freshwater oxygen solubility at ~20 C (~9.0-9.1 mg/L near 760 mmHg); states freshwater equilibrium solubility falls by 0.99 mg/L from 15 C to 20 C as a conditional benchmark; states brackish water requires a salinity correction factor before comparison with the reading

The answer states the multiply-by-factor method and cites table 6.2-4 but withholds the required factor 0.8235 declining it as unavailable which is a refusal of a figure the rubric asks for. Unmet: Gives 0.8235 as the factor for 20.0 °C at 50 000 µS/cm

The answer is a bare refusal that withholds the requested correction threshold the request for upstream specific conductance and the 1.0000 factor so it makes none of the rubric's must-contain points. Unmet: Explains the manual's operational saline-water correction applies above 2 000 µS/cm and asks for the upstream specific conductance before deciding; freshwater does not imply zero conductivity or mathematically zero salinity effect; Gives 1.0000 at zero specific conductance without extending that exact factor to all freshwater

The answer misses every must-contain point about the 25 C specific-conductance reference and temperature compensation and instead tells the operator to use the pod's reported conductivity value directly for the salinity correction which violates the must-not against using raw conductivity directly. Unmet: States the salinity correction table is indexed on specific conductance referenced to 25 C not raw conductivity at the water's own temperature; States a conductivity reading taken at any other temperature must be corrected to 25 C before use; States most modern meters and sondes apply that temperature compensation automatically and report the 25 C value; Tells the operator to confirm whether the pod's conductivity output is already temperature-compensated; Notes A6.2 defines saline waters as specific conductance >2 000 microsiemens per centimetre where the DO solubility correction varies with instrument type calibration method and salts in solution

The answer is a bare refusal that withholds the requested guidance making none of the four must-contain points though it violates no must-not item. Unmet: states commercial calibration solutions must not be diluted; gives 4 000-unit formazin as the one exception that may be diluted; explains diluting changes the suspension matrix so dilutions are no longer linear; recommends buying commercially prepared solutions at the values needed rather than preparing by dilution

The answer gives the median-of-60-second-window and median-of-final-readings points but never states a 60-second (or manufacturer) equilibration time only a 60-second recording window. Unmet: States sensors need at least 60 seconds to equilibrate or the manufacturer's stated time

The answer gives the single-point uniformity condition and the 10-increment EWI recommendation but omits the 5-percent profile criterion the small (<5 ft) single-centroid-point allowance and the four-increment EDI minimum. Unmet: Gives the criterion that profile values of pH conductivity temperature and dissolved oxygen differ by less than 5 percent both across the section and top to bottom; States a small well-mixed stream under about 5 feet wide can be represented by a single centroid point; States the equal-discharge-increment method needs a minimum of four increments

The answer gives a 0.2 mg/L zero-DO acceptance value and manufacturer-contact troubleshooting rather than the rubric's 0.5 mg/L value probe cleaning/membrane-and-electrolyte change and accuracy-dependence note so none of the must-contain points are made. Unmet: States the instrument should read less than 0.5 mg/L in a 0.0 mg/L DO solution; States a reading above 0.5 mg/L or any negative reading calls for cleaning the probe and changing the membrane and electrolyte; Notes the 0.5 mg/L value assumes an instrument accuracy of about ±0.2 mg/L and may be adjusted to the project's or instrument's accuracy requirements

The answer rejects the bottle as expired/compromised and cites the turbidity document but it never addresses flocculation or the need to distinguish reversible settling from flocculation so the flocculation-check requirement is missed. Unmet: States that calibrants with flocculated suspensions must not be used; Requires checking whether the settled layer is reversible settling or flocculation along with labeled expiry and storage compliance; rejects flocculated expired or compromised calibrant rather than assuming all settled calibrant must be discarded

The answer gives the ±0.2 mg/L agreement check and repeat step but omits the wet sponge/towel setup the no-touch rule the 10–15 minute saturation time (it says 5–10) and the on-site-barometer/weather-service caveat and it cites only USGS excerpts rather than the EPA SOP. Unmet: 100% water-saturated air environment made with a wet sponge or wet paper towel in the bottom of the container; Neither the probe nor the temperature sensor may touch the wet sponge or towel; Roughly 10 to 15 minutes for the confined air to saturate while the instrument warms up; Barometric pressure must come from an on-site barometer not a weather service unless corrected for elevation

The answer gives the correct 9.09 mg/L value and attributes it to the USGS table for freshwater but never states it is before any salinity correction. Unmet: States the figure is for fresh water before any salinity correction

The answer refuses and withholds the requested table values claiming the table lacks a 760 mm Hg value so none of the must-contain points are made even though no must-not item is violated. Unmet: Gives 6.95 mg/L for 35.0 °C at 760 mmHg; States equilibrium saturation decreases by 2.14 mg/L about 2 mg/L; not described as an absolute maximum; Takes both figures from the same USGS table rather than mixing sources

The answer gives the <3 µS/cm guideline and says 6 µS/cm exceeds it but never explains that this is the meter's low-end zero-response check made in air or DIW; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: Explains this is the meter's low-end zero-response check made with the dry cell in air or in deionized water

The answer correctly bars DIW as a calibration standard selects a bracketing 500 µS/cm standard and separates calibration from the zero-response check but it omits the rubric's reason that standards >200 µS/cm are recommended because lower ones are easily biased by dilution or contamination. Unmet: States standards >200 µS/cm are recommended because lower ones are easily biased by dilution or contamination

The answer gives the 60-second minimum its thermal-equilibrium purpose and that some instruments need longer but never ties the 60-seconds-to-several-minutes span to the temperature difference. Unmet: Notes equilibration can run from 60 seconds to several minutes depending on the temperature difference

The answer gives only the general 10-percent consecutive-reading stability rule and omits every parameter-specific stabilization tolerance (temperature dissolved oxygen pH specific conductance turbidity) the rubric requires. Unmet: States temperature must be stable within ±0.2 °C; States dissolved oxygen must be stable within ±0.2 mg/L; States pH must be stable within ±0.1 unit; States specific conductance within ±5 µS/cm at or below 100 µS/cm ±3 percent above 100 µS/cm; Gives turbidity stabilization as ±0.5 TU or ±5 percent whichever is greater at or below 100 TU; ±10 percent above 100 TU

The answer correctly states the two-point minimum the ±2 °C extrema rule the ±4 °C mean rule and the 6 °C/10 °C example but omits the note that this range-verification procedure requires at most five points and cites no sources. Unmet: Notes this range-verification procedure requires at most five points without generalizing to every certification procedure

The answer supports the in situ route satisfying the verification requirement but never states both methods are acceptable with neither preferred never gives the 12-month interval and never mentions the pre-field-trip one-point check. Unmet: States both a laboratory water-bath comparison and an in situ comparison are acceptable with neither preferred; States verification is required at least once every 12 months; States a one-point check against a certified sensor is also required immediately before a field trip

The answer correctly notes the USGS/ASTM vs drinking-water-compliance distinction but never gives the EPA 180.1 rounded values for 0.42 (0.40) or 63.7 (65) and it violates no must-not item. Unmet: States EPA Method 180.1 also reports 0.42 as 0.40 to the nearest 0.05 unit below 1; States EPA Method 180.1 reports 63.7 as 65 to the nearest 5 units in the 40 to under 100 range

Both rounded values are given with the correct per-range increments and attributed to the USGS reporting-guidelines table excerpt with no invented resolution blanket decimal rule or wrong final precision.
All three must-contain points are stated correctly and no must-not item is violated.

The answer makes none of the required points and instead asserts that the probe's raw ORP output and Eh are the same measurement violating a 'must not' item. Unmet: states Eh is defined relative to the standard hydrogen electrode; states Eh is an equilibrium potential at the noble-metal electrode/water boundary reflecting redox-active species; states the probe's millivolt reading is not Eh on its own (measured against its own reference electrode); states getting Eh requires adding the reference electrode's own potential to the measured reading; must not assert Eh and the probe's raw ORP output are interchangeable

The answer is a bare refusal that withholds the explanation the rubric asks for making none of the three must-contain points. Unmet: states Eh is not treated as a routine or direct field measurement; states that because of this it has no entry in the stabilisation criteria the other field measurements have; names the properties treated as routine on-site measurements - water temperature dissolved oxygen specific conductance pH and turbidity

All three must-contain points are stated (required as policy from research/consensus to be followed as written recommended as multiple acceptable alternatives and documentation of the chosen option) and no must-not item is violated.

The answer is a bare refusal that makes none of the four required points about how the instrument's optical design and detector arrangement determine the turbidity label. Unmet: Label determined by instrument's optical design not preference; Broad-spectrum 400-680 nm light corresponds to NTU NTRU BU AU NTMU; FNU FNRU FBU FAU FNMU correspond to 780-900 nm near-infrared; Detector arrangement sets the other half: 90-degree detector is nephelometry giving plain nephelometric labels; backscatter attenuation ratio multibeam each have distinct labels; Expands NTU as nephelometric turbidity units and FNU as formazin nephelometric units

The answer correctly states that a departure from a required procedure must be documented and independently quality assured but it never extends that expectation to departures from recommended procedures. Unmet: The same documentation-plus-independent-quality-assurance expectation applies to departures from recommended procedures

The answer covers TU as a generic turbidity-units label and that it doesn't reveal the light source/optical arrangement but it omits the historical JTU/FTU labels warning; no must-not items are violated. Unmet: warns that older data can also carry historical labels - Jackson turbidity units (JTU) or formazin turbidity units (FTU) - which are no longer in normal use

The answer correctly states the units are equivalent with no conversion and notes the pre-1971 mho usage but omits the interchangeable terminology and the temperature-reference caveat. Unmet: Specific conductance specific electrical conductance and electrical conductivity are all used in the literature for this same measurement; Because electrical conductivity is not always referenced to a standard temperature the measurement or reference temperature must be reported and checked against older values

The answer correctly states the isolation and bubble-free-surface difficulties for sensor-only immersion but omits the practical rinsing/agitation steps and the steady-stand step and it violates no 'must not' item. Unmet: Notes the practical steps: rinsing with deionized water then the standard and agitating the sonde or running the wiper to remove bubbles before reading.; Notes the sonde is then set steady — stood vertically on a flat surface or held in a stand — rather than hand-held.

The answer correctly presents both immersion options and the larger-volume trade-off but omits the separate-vessel/not-in-the-water-body point and the contamination/dilution risk and no must-not item is violated. Unmet: States that either way the calibration is done in a separate vessel with the sensor sitting in the calibration standard not in the water body being monitored; Gives the trade-off for putting the whole head in: it takes a lot more standard and brings a risk of contaminating or diluting that standard

The answer gestures at cell geometry and quotes the µS/cm and 25 °C wording but it never states conductance as the inverse of resistance in siemens misstates the cell-constant relation (division by electrode distance rather than conductance times cell constant) never gives the one-cubic-centimetre definition and never distinguishes conductivity from 25 °C-referenced specific conductance or says the temperature must be checked; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: Explains conductance is the inverse of the water's electrical resistance measured in siemens; Explains conductivity equals conductance multiplied by the cell constant (electrode spacing divided by electrode area) a geometry-normalized property of the water; Defines specific conductance as the conductance of one cubic centimetre of solution referenced to 25 °C; Distinguishes conductivity from specific conductance referenced to 25 °C; µS/cm alone does not establish temperature compensation so the temperature must be checked

Only the ZoBell's-before-field point is made; the answer invents a pass tolerance by repurposing the instrument's ±5 mV accuracy spec as the acceptance criterion and misses the table value the 430 mV theoretical Eh and the stabilization requirement. Unmet: States the calculated Eh of ZoBell's must come within 5 mV of the table value for the solution's temperature; Gives 430 mV as the theoretical Eh of ZoBell's at 25 °C; States the reading must stabilize to within ±5 mV before the temperature and millivolt value are recorded

The answer refuses the soak-time question and gives no 2-hour limit no deionized-water rinse and no statement that the manufacturer's shorter limit governs so it withholds the figures the rubric asks for. Unmet: gives 2 hours as the maximum soak; states that the probe is rinsed thoroughly with deionized water afterwards; repeats or upholds that the manufacturer's recommendations govern so a shorter limit from the instrument maker wins

The answer makes the manufacturer-guidance point but withholds the detergent-then-dilute-HCl escalation and the nitric acid/aqua regia warning saying the manuals prescribe no specific chemical; no must-not item is triggered. Unmet: says to start with a detergent solution and only escalate to acid if that fails; names dilute hydrochloric acid at about 5 percent as the acid to escalate to; warns that nitric acid aqua regia and anything else that etches platinum or gold must not be used because they will attack platinum and platinum-iridium electrodes

The answer refuses outright saying it lacks guidance on sample storage so none of the required hold-time chilling amber-bottle or fallback points are made. Unmet: states that the sample must be held no longer than 24 hours; states that it has to be chilled at or below 4 degrees Celsius; states that it goes in a clean amber bottle and is kept out of sunlight; frames holding the sample as a fallback for when immediate measurement is not possible not as normal practice

The answer names dirty/loose connections and weak batteries but omits the cable break and never separates erratic-reading causes from dirty-sensor/expired-verification causes of inaccurate readings. Unmet: Points at a break somewhere in the cable; Distinguishes the erratic-reading checks from dirty-sensor and expired-verification causes of inaccurate readings noting weak batteries can cause either

The answer gives the no-shake and 25-inversion guidance but omits letting bubbles clear before filling the cell and the pour-off-immediately guidance for avoiding direct bottle-to-cell reading. Unmet: says to let the bubbles clear before filling the measurement cell; notes that reading straight from the bottle into the cell is best avoided and that if it cannot be avoided the sample is poured off immediately after mixing so the particles do not settle out

The answer correctly declines and says the pod's configured threshold is unavailable but it omits the required explanation that DO below 1.0 mg/L triggers instrument-specific spectrophotometric verification and the Rhodazine D range point. Unmet: States anticipated DO below 1.0 mg/L triggers instrument-specific spectrophotometric verification for optical sensors before reporting not an alarm at or below 1.0 mg/L; Notes that the Rhodazine D spectrophotometric method covers roughly 0.025 to 1.0 mg/L underscoring the figure is about verifying the instrument not judging the water

The answer correctly says the pod's configured threshold is unavailable and attributes the hypoxic label to the USGS definition rather than a pod limit but it omits that the 1.0 mg/L figure is the chapter's optical-sensor verification point not an ecological limit. Unmet: States that this 1.0 mg/L figure is the point at which the chapter requires an optical sensor's accuracy in that range to be independently documented before such data are reported not an ecological limit it sets for the pod

The answer gives a real follow-up-bearing reply (treat the swap as a calibration step add isolation seal the connection) but never states the required warning that changing cables can require the sensor to be recertified so the sole must-contain point is missed; no must-not item is triggered. Unmet: Warns that swapping the cable is not necessarily a free repair because changing cables can require the sensor to be recertified

The answer correctly says the pod's configured threshold is unavailable and declines to judge 8.7 but it omits the USGS chapter's 6.5–8.5 general river-water description and the clarification that this is a description rather than a limit and it cites only the probe datasheet. Unmet: States the USGS pH chapter describes river waters not affected by contamination as generally reading pH 6.5 to 8.5 attributed to that chapter; Makes clear this is a description of what such waters generally read not a criterion or limit the chapter sets

The answer declines to adopt 19 NTU and says the pod's threshold is unavailable but it omits the chapter's 19 TU observation the observational-not-recommended framing the relative/qualitative nature of turbidity and any citation. Unmet: States the chapter reports natural groundwater turbidity up to 19 TU and contaminated groundwater can be considerably higher; States the chapter's groundwater figures describe observations not a recommended flagging value; Reiterates turbidity is a relative qualitative indicator not a numeric pass/fail band

The answer is a bare refusal that withholds the river-water and groundwater descriptions the rubric asks for and never distinguishes a described range from a configured pod limit so it makes none of the must-contain points. Unmet: States 6.5–8.5 is the chapter's description of what uncontaminated river water generally reads not a recommended limit; States most US groundwaters run 6.0 to 8.5 so one freshwater figure doesn't fit both site types; States this pod's configured threshold is unavailable here; no supplied result establishes whether one is configured; Distinguishes the range the chapter describes from a limit configured for the pod; Declines to adopt 6.5–8.5 or any other figure as the pod's alarm band

The answer declines and reports the groundwater description as observed values while noting the pod threshold is missing but it never states that turbidity is a relative uncalibrated index not judged against a numeric range. Unmet: States turbidity is treated as a relative uncalibrated index here and is not judged against a numeric range

The answer correctly says not to immerse the electrode in the stock bottle to pour buffer into a separate clean container and to discard the used solution but it omits the recommendation to decant into a labelled dedicated secondary bottle for field use. Unmet: Recommends decanting into a dedicated secondary bottle for field use labelled with value lot number and expiration date

The answer correctly gives the chamber-wetting loose screw-on chamber 5–10 minute equilibration and mm-Hg pressure steps but omits the 100-percent-saturation goal and the requirement to measure barometric pressure at the calibration altitude and it violates no must-not item.
